tagline: Follow Green Bay’s shore between a restored lighthouse and preserved timberland.
intro: The Hidden Coast follows M-35 for 64 miles between Gladstone and Menominee, along Little Bay de Noc and Green Bay. Most of M-35 is two lanes, but the shared US-2/US-41 stretch between Gladstone and Escanaba is a four-lane divided highway. Michigan’s transportation department designated this recreational heritage route in 2007. In announcing it, MDOT’s James Lake highlighted the shoreline’s parks, waterways, forests, trails, harbors and campgrounds.

Part of the modern road follows the earlier Sault and Green Bay Trail between Menominee and Escanaba. That Native American footpath continued toward Sault Ste. Marie and Green Bay, wide enough for travelers moving single file. The highway number came later: by 1930, M-35 had extended south from Gladstone through Escanaba and along a new shoreline road to Cedar River, replacing M-91 farther south.

Heading south from Gladstone, follow Little Bay de Noc and cross the Escanaba River near its mouth. M-35 leaves the shared highway in Escanaba and takes Lake Shore Drive toward Green Bay. At the Delta–Menominee county line, the southbound drive crosses from Eastern to Central time, continuing along the coast toward Cedar River and the southern end of the route. Continue through Cedar River and past Wells State Park to Menominee’s Y-shaped junction with US-41 near John Henes Park.

moments.title: Gladstone
moments.text: At Gladstone, the Hidden Coast designation ends where M-35 leaves US-2 and US-41 at Fourth Avenue North. The city occupies a small projection into Little Bay de Noc, which opens into Green Bay. Its waterfront includes Van Cleve Park, with a boardwalk, white-sand beach and harbor. During the 1860s and early 1870s, Gladstone shipped lumber, coal, copper and iron ore. The numbered highway continues inland northwest from here, while the coastal byway leads south toward Escanaba. The Days River Trails offer hiking and biking in spring, summer and fall, with cross-country skiing their main winter use.
moments.notice: Van Cleve Park has a boardwalk, white-sand beach and harbor.

moments.title: Sand Point Lighthouse, Escanaba
moments.text: Sand Point’s brick tower faces landward, and the reason for that orientation is unknown. The light first shone in May 1868 to guide shipping and warn of sand shoals extending into Little Bay de Noc. An offshore automated light replaced it in 1939; the old lighthouse became Coast Guard housing, its tower lowered and lantern room removed. The Delta County Historical Society later restored the building using its 1867 plans. The replacement lantern room came from Poverty Island, and the replacement lens from Menominee Pier Light. Those fittings replaced originals that had not been saved.
moments.notice: The tower faces the land rather than the water.

moments.title: Cedar River
moments.text: Cedar River meets Green Bay at the community of the same name, which began with a sawmill in 1854. Just south, Wells State Park preserves timberland once owned by lumbermen. Sam Crawford deliberately spared a stand of virgin timber while logging hemlock among pine stumps. John Walter Wells later bought the land; his children donated 335 acres to Michigan in 1925 to establish a park. Civilian Conservation Corps crews added trails and buildings using local limestone, granite and timber. The park’s group camp includes rustic cabins from that work.
